newsitem.title: USA: New obstacles seen in multiple sclerosis research.
newsitem.headline: New obstacles seen in multiple sclerosis research.

text.p: Scientists have found some hints that an experimental approach to treating multiple sclerosis may actually make the disease worse.
In research appearing Friday in the journal Science, they report as well that some of the theories about what goes awry in the immune system to cause the disease may be wrong.

"The results ... are troublesome. They imply that it may be problematic to apply these strategies to humans," wrote Henry McFarland of the National Institutes of Health in an essay accompanying the research in Science.

In MS, the immune system wrongly attacks the insulation, called myelin, that protects nerves in the brain and spinal cord. Because the immune system is attacking its own body, it is called an "auto-immune" reaction.

The experiment led by Dr. Claude Genain and Dr. Stephen Hauser at the University of California at San Francisco and elsewhere involved a technique known as "immune deviation." The idea was to build up tolerance in the immune system by giving low doses of the protein that causes the auto-immune reaction in the first place.

In animal tests the idea seemed to work during the treatment, but once the treatment stopped, the MS actually got worse, Genain and Hauser found. They did not say that this type of research should be stopped but said it must be closely monitored and proceed slowly.

In addition their experiment raised questions about a theory about how two types of immune cells contribute to the auto-immune process. It had been thought that a "good" type of T-cell helped control inflammation and a "bad" T-cell promoted it but that seems to be wrong.
